# 1 Clement Chapter 36 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 1 Clement 36 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/1CL_036_page_001.jpg

---

## Chapter 36

**36:1** This is the way, beloved, in which we found our salvation: Jesus Christ, the high priest of our offerings, the guardian and helper of our weakness.

**36:2** Through him we gaze into the heights of heaven; through him we behold as in a mirror his blameless and most exalted face; through him the eyes of our heart have been opened; through him our foolish and darkened understanding blossoms toward his wonderful light; through him the Master has willed that we taste immortal knowledge — he who is "the radiance of his glory and the very stamp of his being, upholding all things by the word of his power" — at whose right hand the angels and archangels and powers and thrones and dominions are set, giving worship.

**36:3** Through the greatness and excellence of his beauty the six-winged and many-eyed ones stand before him — the seraphim and the cherubim — crying: "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Hosts; the whole creation is full of his glory."

**36:4** And we too, gathered together in concord in one place, let us cry out earnestly to him as from one mouth, that we may become partakers of his great and glorious promises.

**36:5** For it says: "Eye has not seen, and ear has not heard, and it has not arisen in the heart of man, the things which he has prepared for those who wait for him."

---

## Translator's Note

Chapter 36 is the christological climax of the first half of 1 Clement and one of the most important christological texts outside the NT. Its connections to the Epistle to the Hebrews are striking: "high priest of our offerings" (cf. Heb 2:17; 3:1; 4:14); "radiance of his glory and the very stamp of his being, upholding all things by the word of his power" (cf. Heb 1:3 almost verbatim). Whether Clement is quoting Hebrews, Hebrews is using Clement, or both draw on a common hymnic source is a major scholarly question. The five-fold "through him" (*di' autou*) anaphora (v. 2) creates a soaring christological meditation. The Trisagion (v. 3) appears again here (cf. ch. 34:6). SOPHIA follows LOGOS in "the very stamp of his being" for *charakter tēs hypostaseōs* (cf. Heb 1:3).

---

*SOPHIA represents the consensus translation, balancing literalness and clarity.*
